question: Is it permissible for men to dye their hair or beard, especially with black?
answer:
So, dyeing the hair with henna, or with other natural dyes that don't imitate your natural hair color... Now, the hadith mentions black, and the books of fiqh mention black, because black was the default hair color in the Middle East. And so when the books of fiqh mention black as the controversy, what they mean is the hair color that you naturally have. So if your hair is already yellow or blonde or red or whatever it is, then the controversy would be: can you use a dye that matches your original hair color? Henna, which is reddish in nature, you know is not your hair color. So **it is sunnah to dye the hair with henna, or with other natural dyes that are clearly not the original color of your hair.** Our Prophet ﷺ would regularly dye his beard with henna.

And we're also familiar with the fact that the Shari'ah does say that during times of war and confrontation, the army should definitely look powerful and young, and whatever that takes, dyeing your hair, that's also something that is good. The question, though, is: outside of those situations, is it permissible for a man in particular to dye his hair or his beard black, meaning the color that it originally was, if your hair color is black?

And the reason why there's a controversy is a famous hadith and incident of the seerah: the Prophet ﷺ greeted the father of Abu Bakr ibn Abi Quhafa. When he saw Abu Quhafa, his hair was completely white. He said to the people in the entourage, "Take him back and change the white, but avoid black. Avoid black." Now, based on this, which is an authentic hadith, the scholars differed. Is that avoidance for a particular reason, or is it unconditional? Is that avoidance obligatory, or is it recommended? All of these are controversies.

And again, because this is the short round, I'll just quickly go over the three opinions you have in this regard. The Shafi'i school was the strictest, and if you're from Malaysia, I'm assuming you're following the Shafi'i school. The Shafi'i school said that it is haram for a man to dye his beard or his hair black; you don't do that. The majority position, which is the Hanafi, the Maliki and the Hanbali schools, said that it is not haram, but it is better to avoid. It is makruh; you're not sinful, as long as (everybody said this) there's no deception.

Now, the deception here really comes in... The scholars give the primary example; this is before the age of IDs and knowing your birthdays and whatnot. When you go and propose, you are judged on your outer appearance, and your age is basically derived from your looks. So if you're 60 years old and you pretend you're 35, this is a type of deceit. And nowadays, by the way, it's almost impossible to do, because there are IDs and birthdays and whatnot. But my point being, back in those days there was this notion of deception: you hide your age by your appearance. Clearly, any deceit is not allowed in the Shari'ah: "Whoever deceives us is not of us. Whoever cheats us is not of us."

Suppose there's no cheating. Suppose you just want to do it for the sake of looking more handsome, looking younger. You're already married, or you're not looking to get married, or whatever it might be. So the Shafi'is said it is haram. The Hanafis, Malikis and Hanbalis said that it is not haram, but it's better to avoid; it's makruh. Some said it is strongly makruh, but the majority said it is makruh, meaning you are not sinful. By makruh, I don't mean to trivialize; I'm simply saying you are not sinful, but they discouraged it. They said it's better not to do.

And a third opinion said that it is completely permissible, mubah; there is not even karahah in it. They based this on the fact that many of the Sahaba and Tabi'un, it is reported, would dye their hair black. Ibn al-Qayyim reports in his Zad al-Ma'ad; Ibn al-Qayyim says it is authentically narrated that the two grandsons of the Prophet ﷺ, Hasan and Husayn, would dye their beards black. And Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas would dye his beard black; this is reported in al-Tabarani. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, the famous one of al-'Asharah al-Mubashsharah, would dye his beard black. So if it was something that the Sahaba thought to be haram, they wouldn't do it in public, with everybody seeing it and nobody making inkar or saying no to them.

So inshallah ta'ala, look, Allah knows best, but it's not haram, or else the Sahaba would not have done it. But maybe it's makruh. Especially if there's an element of deceit involved, then for sure it becomes sinful and haram. **If there is no deception involved, if you avoid it, it is better, and if you do it, it is not sinful.** There is no doubt that the one who avoids these things out of piety will be more rewarded. Nonetheless, at the end of the day, it is not sinful.

By the way, this is for a man. As for a woman, inshallah the correct position is that married women for sure, if they want to appear beautiful for their husbands, the Shari'ah actually encourages it. We want women to look beautiful for their husbands. We want them to put on make-up and whatever it might be, and do the hair and whatever, so that their husbands find them beautiful and attractive. And so the ruling that we're talking about is for men's beards and whatnot. And even then, as we said, the majority say that it is makruh. And Allah 'azza wa jall knows best.
